text: Once an SLA Definition's Start condition is met, its task_sla instance begins counting elapsed time against the duration target. From there it moves toward exactly one of two outcomes: Stop, because the Stop condition fired in time, or Breach, because the duration elapsed first.

Everything in between is where Pause matters most. Pause suspends time accumulation without ending the SLA — the clock resumes exactly where it left off the moment the Pause condition stops matching, rather than resetting or continuing to run.

The real, common Pause case is State = On Hold with Hold Reason = Awaiting Caller. A well-implemented Pause condition is built on exactly that combination, so time spent waiting on the customer to call back doesn't eat into the team's resolution target.

A Pause condition scoped too broadly — pausing on On Hold regardless of reason — can just as easily hide time the team should legitimately be held accountable for, like waiting on an internal change the team itself is responsible for scheduling.

The Stop condition, typically State = Resolved, ends the clock and marks the instance Achieved if the target wasn't exceeded. If duration reaches one hundred percent before Stop fires, the instance is marked Breached, usually after warning notifications at fifty, seventy-five, and ninety percent.

SLA duration math is schedule-aware. An SLA Definition references a real cmn_schedule record like '8-5 Weekdays' — so a 4-hour SLA opened at 4 PM on a Friday doesn't breach that evening, it pauses for the weekend and breaches around noon on Monday.

Choosing the wrong schedule, or no schedule at all for a target that should be business-hours-only, is as serious an error as a bad Start or Pause condition. Next up: SLA Reporting, turning the task_sla table into real breach-rate and trend data.
